title: Seed Travelers
goal: Your kid collects seeds and pods from outside and solves a small mystery hiding in each one: how does this thing travel? Plants can't walk, so every seed has a trick for getting away from its parent and finding a new place to grow. Some fly, some float, some hitch a ride, some just drop. Once a kid can read those tricks, a handful of seeds turns into a set of tiny inventions, each one a solution to the same problem.
need: A handful of different seeds or pods: maple keys, burrs, acorns, dandelion puffs, dry grass heads
An old sock or fuzzy sweater, and a bowl of water
A notebook, and a yard, park or trail where things grow

lesson.text: The shape of a seed almost always tells you how it moves. The skill is reading a feature, guessing its job, then testing it.

model.line: This maple key has a thin, papery wing on one side.
I think it travels by wind.
Dropped from shoulder height, it spun like a helicopter and drifted a metre away.
The wing slows the fall, so the wind can carry it away from the tree.

lesson.modelNote: The wing is the clue the first line skipped. Guess its job, drop it from shoulder height, and the seed answers.

howTo.intro: The trap is naming the answer: say 'that one flies' and the mystery's gone. Ask what the shape might be for, and let the tests decide. Seeds stay out of mouths.

plan.what: The helicopter warm-up, the seed hunt, look closely and guess (Steps 1 and 2).
Sort them, then test the fliers, stickers and floaters (Steps 3 and 4).

troubleshoot.a: Try the kitchen too: a dried bean, a sunflower seed, an apple seed, a strawberry. Fall is the best season for a seed hunt.
That's worth talking about. Test it both ways and let the result decide.

steps.title: Fly a paper helicopter
steps.why: A quick spinning toy, then the hunt for real seeds that do the same.
steps.kid: Cut a strip of paper, split the top into two flaps, fold them opposite ways, fold the bottom up for weight and drop it from up high: it spins down slowly. That's the same trick a maple key uses. Then head outside and gather 5 to 10 different seeds or pods. The more different, the better: a spinning maple key, a sticky burr, a heavy acorn, a fluffy dandelion.
steps.you: Help make the helicopter, then steer them toward variety on the hunt and let them lead. Seeds are everywhere once you look: in cracks, under trees, stuck to your own socks. Longer wings usually fall slower: more paper pushing against the air.
ask: Why did the paper helicopter fall so slowly?
Which seed looks the strangest, and why might it be shaped like that?
steps.tip: Check your socks after walking through tall grass for seeds that hitched a ride, and check for ticks at the same time.

levels.explore: Fly the helicopter, then collect 3 or 4 different seeds.
levels.develop: Collect 5 to 10 seeds with different shapes.
levels.extend: Fly one with longer wings too. Which falls slower?

steps.title: Look closely and guess
steps.why: Your kid reads each seed's features and predicts how it travels.
steps.kid: Your kid examines each seed: is it light or heavy? Does it have wings, hooks, fluff or a hard shell? Then, like the maple key example, they guess how each one travels: on the wind, on water, on an animal, or just by dropping. They write the guesses down.
steps.you: Ask what they see, not what it's called. Take every guess seriously, right or wrong: the tests will check them. A magnifying glass or your phone's zoom helps. For Extend: animals eat the fruit, carry the seeds off and drop them in their droppings.
ask: Does it have anything that looks built for a job?
Does this look like it could fly, or is it too heavy?
steps.tip: They'll be unsure about some, and that's perfect. The uncertain seeds are exactly the ones worth testing.

levels.explore: Feel one seed: light or heavy, fluffy or hard? Guess fly or drop.
levels.develop: Note a feature on each seed, and guess between all four travel types.
levels.extend: Why might a seed hide inside tasty fruit, like an apple pip?

steps.title: Sort the travellers
steps.why: Your kid groups the seeds by how they travel.
steps.kid: Your kid lays the seeds out and sorts them into piles: wind travellers, water travellers, animal hitchhikers, and droppers. Some might fit two piles, and that's worth talking about.
steps.you: Let them build the groups their own way, then ask them to defend a few choices. Acorns drop, but squirrels and jays carry and bury them, so they're animal travellers too, which the sock test can't show.
ask: Which seeds belong together, and why?
Are there any that could go in two groups?
steps.tip: Flag the seeds they're unsure about. Those go first in the tests.

levels.extend: Find one that fits two piles. Which trick does most of the work?

steps.title: Test them
steps.why: Drop, stick and float: proving the guesses.
steps.kid: Your kid tests each group. Fliers: drop each one from the same height and watch whether it spins and drifts or plops straight down. Hitchhikers: brush each against an old sock and see if it grabs on. Floaters: drop each into a bowl of water, wait an hour, then stir. Many seeds float at first; water travellers stay up longest. They mark which guesses were right and fix the wrong ones.
steps.you: Help set a fair drop (same height for every seed) and set up the sock and the water bowl. A gentle puff of breath or a fan makes the wind test even clearer. Slow fallers spend longer in the air, so the fan usually pushes them farthest.
ask: Did it spin and drift, or drop straight down?
Did it stick to the sock? Did it float?
steps.tip: A wrong guess that gets corrected teaches more than a lucky right one. Celebrate both.

levels.explore: Drop one seed and try the sock test with another.
levels.develop: Test a few seeds in all three tests and compare.
levels.extend: Time each flier's fall, then drop it by a fan. Do slow fallers drift farthest?

steps.title: Design the ultimate seed
steps.why: Your kid ranks the travellers, then invents a seed of their own.
steps.kid: Your kid picks the best traveller and says why, using what they saw in the tests. Then the deeper question: is there a perfect seed? A sticky seed rides an animal for miles but can't fly. A fluffy seed flies beautifully but goes nowhere on a still day. Finally, they design their own seed: draw it, name it, explain how it travels, and name its one weakness.
steps.you: Push their thinking with 'what does it give up?' For Extend there's no right answer: big seeds get a strong start, tiny ones reach more places.
ask: What does your best traveller give up to be so good at it?
Where would your invented seed struggle?
steps.tip: Realising there's no perfect seed, only seeds that are great at one kind of travel, is a surprisingly grown-up idea.

levels.explore: Pick the best traveller, then draw a seed and say how it moves.
levels.develop: Rank several with reasons, then design a seed that borrows two real features.
levels.extend: With only so much food, should a plant make a few big seeds or lots of tiny ones? Design for one.

conclusion.headline: Seed shapes are clues now.
conclusion.text: After a walk through tall grass, check your socks together. They'll pick off what's stuck, tell you it travels by animal, and point to the hooks that prove it. Then hand them a seed they've never seen and wait for a guess before you look it up.
conclusion.celebrate: When a seed they called a flier plopped straight down, say: 'You changed your answer the second the seed proved you wrong. I loved watching that.'
extensions: Go on a seed hunt in a different season and compare
Plant a few of the seeds and see which ones grow
Count the hitchhikers on your clothes after a walk through tall grass
Build a paper seed and see how far you can make it fly

signs: They pick up seeds on walks and guess how they travel
They group things by what they do, not just how they look
A strange shape gets a 'what's it for?'
makeItReal: Plant the seeds you collected in labelled pots, with each one's travel group on the label, and check every few days to see which ones come up.
